common_name: Captain of the Blues Sweet Pea (Violet-Blue Victorian Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight, then sow as early as soil can be worked; fall sowing suits mild-winter regions.

directions: This Victorian-era grandiflora, dating to the 1870s-1880s, bears a rich violet-blue standard over lighter cornflower-blue wings and carries the intense clove fragrance of the earliest sweet pea introductions. Set up trellis or netting at sowing time so the tendrils can grip from the start, since vines resent being handled once tall. Pick blooms every few days through the cool season to prevent pods from forming, which otherwise stops flower production early. Enrich the planting bed with compost before sowing, as this old cultivar flowers best in fertile, evenly moist soil.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Janet Scott Sweet Pea (Pink Fragrant Grandiflora, 1901)

planting.note: Sow directly once soil is workable, or fall-sow in mild climates for larger, earlier-blooming plants.

directions: Introduced in 1901, this grandiflora produces clear rose-pink blooms with an especially strong, sweet perfume that made it a favorite cut flower of the Edwardian era. Provide sturdy netting or twiggy brush at planting so the tendrils have something to grasp immediately, and keep the root zone shaded with mulch while the top grows in full sun. Harvest stems as soon as the lowest florets open to encourage continued branching and bloom. Regular picking and a deep weekly soak in dry spells will extend the flowering season well into summer.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Queen Alexandra Sweet Pea (Scarlet Edwardian Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick and soak seed before sowing as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring.

directions: Named for the queen consort and introduced in the early 1900s, this grandiflora carries vivid scarlet flowers that hold their color well without fading to mauve in heat, a common flaw of older red sweet peas. Erect a trellis or pea netting at sowing so young tendrils can climb without support later, and pinch seedlings once they reach a few inches to encourage bushier, more floriferous growth. Deadhead spent stems continually, since even a few ripening pods will curtail further bloom. A cool root run under mulch helps carry plants through early summer warmth.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Countess Spencer Sweet Pea (Pale Pink, Origin of the Spencer Type, 1901)

planting.note: Sow direct once soil can be worked; where winters stay mild, fall sowing gives earlier, taller plants.

directions: Discovered in 1901 by Silas Cole, head gardener at Althorp, this soft pink sweet pea was the first with the large, ruffled standard that defined the entire Spencer class still grown today. Give plants a tall trellis or netting from the outset, since Spencer-type vines are vigorous climbers that quickly outgrow flimsy supports. Feed lightly with a low-nitrogen fertilizer once buds form to favor bloom over foliage, and pick every stem as it opens to keep the long flowering season going. Rich, deeply worked soil with consistent moisture produces the longest stems for cutting.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: Asta Ohn Sweet Pea (Mauve Heirloom Grandiflora)

planting.note: Nick seed coats and soak overnight before an early spring sowing as soon as the ground is workable.

directions: This early-1900s grandiflora bears smoky mauve-lavender flowers and is regarded among heirloom growers as one of the most powerfully fragrant sweet peas ever raised. Install netting or brushy twigs at sowing so tendrils can climb from the seedling stage onward, and site plants where the scent will drift toward a porch, path, or open window. Keep the flowers cut hard, since this variety sets seed readily and stops blooming quickly once pods are left on the vine. A cool, humus-rich bed with steady moisture keeps stems long and flowering strong into early summer.
sources: Select Seeds heirloom sweet pea catalog
Royal Horticultural Society Lathyrus odoratus cultivar notes

common_name: North Shore Sweet Pea (Deep Blue-Purple Bicolor Spencer)

planting.note: Start in root trainers in late winter where springs are short, or sow direct once soil can be worked.

directions: A modern Spencer-type bred by New Zealand sweet pea specialist Dr. Keith Hammett, this cultivar carries deep navy-blue standards over rich violet-purple wings on long, wiry stems favored by exhibitors. Provide tall netting or string supports at planting, since vigorous Spencer vines quickly reach six to eight feet in good conditions. Pinch young plants once they have three or four true leaves to promote strong basal branching before they begin to climb. Water deeply and consistently through bud formation, as inconsistent moisture is the most common cause of dropped buds in this type.

common_name: Sir Jimmy Shand Sweet Pea (Cerise-Pink and Cream Bicolor Spencer)

planting.note: Start in root trainers in late winter for earliest bloom, or sow direct once soil can be worked.

directions: Bred by Dr. Keith Hammett and named for the Scottish accordionist, this multiple award-winning Spencer type bears bright cerise-pink standards edged around a cream-flushed base, giving each bloom striking two-tone contrast. Set netting or strings in place before sowing so young vines can climb without check, and pinch seedlings early to build a well-branched framework before flowering begins. Keep every open stem cut for the vase, since this heavy-blooming variety will stop setting new flowers quickly if pods are allowed to mature. Feed sparingly with a potassium-rich fertilizer once flowering starts to sustain stem length and color intensity through the season.
